newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France banks on growth as unemployment rises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France banks on growth as unemployment rises.

text.p: The French government, confronted with a further rise in unemployment in the first month of 1997, said on Friday the economy was looking up and this would produce jobs, but shied from predicting when jobless queues would fall.

Despite several positive indicators for stronger growth in the economy at the outset of 1997, Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government is still plagued by the politically thorny issue of record unemployment.

The labour ministry said on Friday unemployment had risen by 18,100 in January to just short of 3.1 million and that the rate of unemployment based on International Labour Organisation (ILO) criteria was stuck at the record 12.7 percent hit in November.

The rise followed a drop of 29,000 in December but economists have dismissed that decrease, and another drop last October, as "statistical blips" and say unemployment is still on the rise. Some say it could reach 13 percent later this year.
The government is hoping for economic growth of at least 2.3 percent in 1997, after a relatively poor 1.3 percent increase in 1996, and banking on the increased growth to create jobs.

So far this year, its predictions of an economic upturn have been bolstered by news of rising consumer spending and surveys showing that French industrialists are more optimistic about the prospects for an increase in production in the coming months, and news that France had another record trade surplus in 1996.

Labour minister Jaques Barrot told state radio on Friday it was still hard to decipher the pattern but that the economy was looking healthier, with rising household spending and exports, and signs companies were starting to reinvest and recruit.
"(Economic) growth is clearly returning -- at what pace is unclear, but things are improving," he told France Inter radio.
"Jobs come from growth. Growth is coming back, consumption and exports are picking up. Company bosses are starting to invest again and then recruiting," he said.

"It's a bit like the tide. In terms of jobs we don't quite know where we stand at the moment, whether the tide is rising or falling. It's tricky because the direction of the waves is not clear," he said. "But in the opening months of 1997 we will probably be stuck with upward and downward spikes," he added.
The January unemployment data showed a drop for the second month in a row in the number of jobless men and women aged 25 or less, with a 1.5 percent drop for men and 0.7 percent for women.

Some economists, however, believe this is partly because of administrative changes under which registration of unemployed is now done at the UNEDIC agency in charge of paying unemployment benefit rather than at the ANPE job search agency.
Young people who have never worked are not entitled to this benefit and may be discouraged from signing on as unemployed at the UNEDIC agency since the administrative changes, they say.

Despite demands that they make employment a top priority, Prime Minister Alain Juppe and President Jacques Chirac are sticking to budget cuts and austerity plans designed to qualify France to join a single European currency in 1999.

Philippe Brossard, an economist at dutch bank ABN Amro in Paris, said the unemployment data could keep up pressure on the Bank of France to trim interest rates further but highlighted the recent batch of positive economic data.

"We had a lot of good news recently. This (jobless data) shows the good news is more for prospects rather than for the current situation. So there may still be some pressure on the Bank of France to try to narrow the gap with German rates," he said.
Consumer spending in France showed a healthy 1.9 percent rise in January, according data released on Wednesday.

The national statistics institute INSEE announced on Friday that a February survey of industrialists showed a second monthly improvement in confidence regarding the likelihood of a pick-up in output after a turnaround in sentiment in a January survey.
